list.listitem: Consider karyotyping girls with unexplained short stature for Turner syndrome. C
Treatment with human growth hormone (hGH) should be initiated as soon as possible. C
Standard therapy includes hGH and estradiol. A
Individuals with Turner syndrome are at higher risk of heart and autoimmune disorders. A

background.definition: The diagnosis of Turner syndrome requires the presence of typical clinical symptoms, such as short stature, along with complete or partial absence of the second sex chromosome, with or without mosaicism. Individuals with a 45, X cell population but without clinical features are not considered to have Turner syndrome.

list.listitem: Approximately 1 in 2500 live-born females.
Twenty-five to 50 per 100,000 females.
Women with Turner syndrome are at higher risk of developing celiac disease (OR 3.29; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.94-5.56).
Women with untreated premature ovarian insufficiency, including Turner syndrome, have a reduced life expectancy, primarily from cardiovascular disease.
Complete or partial absence of one sex chromosome.
Many systems are affected, including short stature, early ovarian failure with infertility, and increased risk for autoimmune diseases.
If there is any remnant of the Y chromosome present, there is a high risk of gonadoblastoma.

Aortic coarctation and bicuspid valve may occur, as well as a high prevalence of ECG conduction and repolarization abnormalities. Aortic dilation, dissection, or rupture may occur in relatively young individuals, and this is often fatal.
Prenatal screening can be done in the first trimester by ultrasound for increased nuchal translucency. If this is abnormal, chorionic villus sampling should be offered. C

Noninvasive prenatal testing using fetal-free DNA in maternal blood can successfully detect sex chromosome aneuploidies, although the positive predictive value of the test for Turner syndrome was lower than that of other sex chromosomal aneuploidies. B

Whole-exome sequencing, a transcriptomics technique for sequencing protein-coding genes which make up about 1% of the human genome, can be used to screen for and diagnose Turner syndrome (including those with low-level mosaicism). A
School-based height screening programs have a low yield (1 in 14,000 to 1 in 50,000), but may nevertheless be cost-effective.
Screen women with Turner syndrome for cardiac risk factors (i.e., blood pressure, smoking, weight, lipid profile, glucose) and offer appropriate management.

Thoracic aorta and cardiac evaluation with a transthoracic echocardiogram and CT/cardiac magnetic resonance scan should be considered within 2 years before planned pregnancy or assisted reproductive therapy in women with Turner syndrome; women with a history of aortic dissection should be advised against pregnancy.
Suspect Turner syndrome in any child with short stature, especially in the presence of typical physical findings. C

The diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype showing 45, X or karyotype and mosaicism of 45, X and 46, XX+45, X along with the presence of typical features such as short stature, cubitus valgus, nuchal folds, and a short fourth metacarpal. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Short stature, but low risk for ovarian failure
No short stature, but deletion of the long arm distal to Xq24

list.listitem: Growth restriction may begin in utero, but growth velocity will remain below the 10th percentile for age group.

Physical exam findings vary, but may include short stature, nuchal folds, low hairline with low set ears, high arched palate, chronic otitis media, cubitus valgus, hyperconvex uplifted nails, nail hypoplasia, and short fourth metacarpal.
Other findings include edema of the hands or feet, multiple pigmented nevi, left-sided cardiac abnormalities (especially coarctation of the aorta or hypoplastic left heart), and a small mandible.
Be alert to aortic dissection in women with TS presenting with chest pain; in one cohort study it was the leading cause of death in 23% of women.
Karyotype 45, X, or mosaicism for 45, X and 46, XX, is necessary but not sufficient for diagnosis.

Prenatal ultrasound for nuchal translucency is used as a screen for genetic abnormalities. If prenatal nuchal translucency is increased, chorionic villus sampling for karyotype should be considered. Ultrasound identification of dorsal foot edema also suggests Turner syndrome.

Single-nucleotide polymorphism-based noninvasive prenatal testing using cell-free DNA from the plasma of pregnant women is available and is highly accurate for detecting some microdeletion syndromes; its place in general population screening is unknown. In one large population study, the positive predictive value for all aneuploidies using this test was 82.9%. In a smaller study, sensitivity and specificity for detection of monosomy X with this test was 90% and 99.9%, respectively. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends that conventional screening methods be used as first-line screening for most women given the limited data on test performance and cost-effectiveness in the general, low-risk obstetric population.
FSH is markedly elevated in 45, X, but less reliably in patients with mosaicism who may have retained ovarian function.

Elevated liver enzymes may be another clue to diagnosis in women with short stature. In one case series of 31 women with short stature and elevated liver enzymes, 27 (87%) had X chromosome abnormalities.
Another study found that liver disease was 4 to 6 times more likely in persons wiith Turner Syndrome.
Consider diagnosis in any girl with unexplained short stature, especially if accompanied by typical physical findings.
Below 3 years of age, order full diagnostic evaluation including karyotype, if height is >2.5 SD below mean for age or if height is between 2 and 2.5 SD below mean with typical physical findings.
If 3 years or older, order full diagnostic evaluation, if height >3 SD below mean for age or if repeated measures are >2.5 SD below mean for age.

The International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group recommend transthoracic echocardiography for infants or children diagnosed with Turner syndrome and a resting ECG and renal ultrasound in all patients on initial diagnosis. They also recommend annual developmental and behavioral screenings until adulthood and neuropsychological assessments at key transitional stages in schooling.
Recombinant human growth hormone (hGH) is effective. Although it will increase the final height achieved, in most cases, height is still below normal. A
Estradiol should be given to induce puberty in girls with ovarian failure. A
Recombinant hGH at 0.3 to 0.375 mg/kg/wk increases short-term growth and final height, although the final height is usually still below normal.

The International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group recommend initiating GH treatment at an early age. Updated 2024 guidelines note that GH treatment can be started as early as age 2 if growth failure has been diagnosed (e.g., below 50th percentile height velocity (HV) observed over 6 months in the absence of other treatable causes of poor growth) or the child is already short or has a strong likelihood of short stature (e.g., short parents and short predicted adult height or already pubertal at the time of diagnosis).
The recommended dose is 45 to 50 µg/kg/day or 1.3 to mg/m2/day (4.0-4.5 IU/m2/day) in most cases, increasing to 68 µg/kg/day (2.0 mg/m2/day) if adult height potential is substantially compromised.

They also recommend the addition of the anabolic–androgenic steroid oxandrolone from age 10 years or older at 0.03 mg/kg/day and maintained below 0.05 mg/kg/day, if the diagnosis of Turner syndrome is delayed and/or adult height outcome is likely to be unsatisfactory with the standard GH dose alone.

The UK Turner Syndrome study compared oxandrolone with placebo starting at 9 years in 92 patients and, after final height had been achieved, saw a mean 4.1 cm (95% CI 1.6-6.6 cm) with active treatment.

More than 90% of patients with Turner syndrome experience gonadal failure. If FSH levels are elevated, treatment is begun at age 12 years with transdermal estradiol 6.25 µg/day via preferably via transdermal patch 5 µg/kg/day with oral 0.25 mg/day an option. The estrogen dose is gradually increased at 6- to 12-month intervals to the adult dose of 100 to 200 µg/day transdermal or 2 to 4 mg/day oral by around age 15 years. Micronized progesterone 100 to 200 mg/day or dydrogesterone 5 to 10 mg/day is added for 12 to 14 days per month after 2 years on low-dose estrogen. If the diagnosis is made later in adolescence or adulthood, estrogen may be started at higher doses and increased more rapidly.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs and 13 cohort studies with 771 patients concluded that estrogen therapy increased bone mineral density and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels (particularly using oral estrogen), with no significant effect on other lipid fractions. Studies had moderate to high risk of bias and it is unclear if these improvements translate into clinically-important changes.

Transdermal estrogens appear to have a more favorable effect on fasting glucose, cholesterol, and whole-body bone mineral density, while oral estrogens have a more favorable influence on LDL-C and HDL-C. In this meta-analysis of four studies, there were no statistically significant differences between oral and transdermal estrogens in all other measured parameters including body mass index, fat mass, fasting insulin, triglycerides, estradiol, or estrone levels. Estrogen treatment should be lifelong.
In one RCT of 40 hypogonadal teenage girls with Turner syndrome, route of estrogen delivery (oral or transdermal) did not differentially affect body composition or lipid concentrations.
Oral contraceptives are best avoided because the dose of synthetic estrogens is too high and the typical synthetic progestin may interfere with optimal breast and uterine development.
If genitourinary symptoms persist despite oral estrogen, consider addition of vaginal estrogen and vaginal lubricants.
Surgery may be needed to correct congenital cardiac and vascular abnormalities.
Recommendations for surgical intervention can be found in the International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group guidelines.

The International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group recommends shared decision-making regarding gonadectomy in all female individuals with Y chromosome material identified on standard karyotyping due to the risk of gonadoblastoma. This is an update from previous recommendations when it was routinely recommended.
Oocyte cryopreservation has been safely performed following ovarian stimulation in women with Turner Syndrome. Multiple cycles may be needed to preserve an adequate number of oocytes.
Girls with Turner syndrome should have an elemental calcium intake >1000 mg daily in the preteen years and 1200 to 1500 mg daily after 11 years of age. This generally requires a supplement.
Counseling on healthy eating habits, exercise, and maintaining a healthy weight is essential.
Many women with Turner syndrome experience decreased self-esteem, particularly those with premature ovarian failure. Psychological intervention may be appropriate.

Counsel patients with Turner syndrome who have aortic dilatation and/or bicuspid aortic valve to report potential symptoms of aortic root dissection including chest, neck, shoulder, back or flank discomfort, particularly if it is of sudden onset and severe.
Authors of a systematic review found a pooled prevalence of ascending aortic dilatation of 23% at a mean pooled age of 29 years. The incidence of aortic dissection was 164 per 100,000 patient years.

Medical treatment, including a beta-blocker, an angiotensin receptor blocker or both, is recommended to reduce dilatation of an enlarged aortic root and/or ascending aorta for girls with Turner syndrome who are ≤16 years of age for whom their ascending aorta TS-specific Z-score is ≥3.0.

There is an increased risk of aortic stenosis and aortic root dilation. A Swedish retrospective matched observational study with 472 women with TS and 2357 controls, aortic dissection was much more common in women with TS (HR 9.1, 95% CI 4.5 to 18.2). All-cause mortality was also higher (HR 2.9, 95% CI 1.9 to 4.4), primarily due to aortic dissection which was the largest cause of death in 23% of patients.
Many women with Turner syndrome have normal intelligence, although many have learning disabilities.
A high rate of ovarian failure causes infertility.
Women with Turner syndrome are also at greater risk of hearing and thyroid problems, celiac disease, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
Vulvar lichen sclerosis also appears to be more frequent in this population.
The risk of gonadoblastoma, brain tumors, and meningioma is increased, but the risk of breast cancer is decreased.

There is an increased prevalence of autoimmune hypothyroidism. In a population study using a dataset of all hospital admissions in England, elevated rate ratios for the 2459 people with Turner syndrome were seen for celiac disease (rate ratio 14.0; 95% CI 10.2-18.8), Crohn's disease (5.3; 3.5-7.8), ulcerative colitis (3.9; 2.3-6.1), hypothyroidism (8.8; 7.8-9.9), and hyperthyroidism (4.9; 3.2-7.1).

Patients with Turner syndrome should be screened with transthoracic echocardiography and magnetic resonance angiography because of the high rate of congenital disease of the aortic valve and aortic root dilation. In the absence of a bicuspid aortic valve or other significant disease at initial screening, the International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group recommends monitoring with one of these tests every 5 years in children, every 10 years in adults, or prior to anticipated pregnancy to evaluate the aorta based on published guidelines.

Patients with Turner syndrome should be screened with LH, FSH, and anti-Mullerian hormone at 8-9 years and annually from approximately 11-12 years. This informs decisions about counseling and referral for fertility preservation as well as future stature and need for hormone therapy.

Levels of anti-Müllerian hormone <−2 SD may be useful for predicting lack of spontaneous puberty in prepubertal girls and imminent premature ovarian insufficiency in women with Turner syndrome and preserved ovarian function.

The International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group recommends, based on low-level evidence, the following: Monitoring height at least every 4 to 6 months during the first year of growth-promoting treatment and at least every 6 months after. Monitoring growth-promoting therapy with insulin-like growth factor (IGF-I) at least annually. If IGF-I value is above 3 SDS, a GH dose decrease is warranted. For an IGF-I value between +2 SDS and +3 SDS, clinical judgment should guide further GH dose selection. Formal audiometric evaluation every 5 years with aggressive treatment of middle-ear disease and otitis media. Screening for hypothyroidism at diagnosis and then annually with (free) T4 and TSH measurements beginning in early childhood. Screening for diabetes annually with HbA1c with or without fasting plasma glucose starting at age of 10 years. Obtaining a lipid profile in individuals who have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular disease starting at age 18 years.

Pregnancy is discouraged in women with aortic root dilation because of increased risk of death during childbirth due to aortic dissection (up to 2%). The risk of death during pregnancy is increased as much as 100-fold. Specific guidance for women with Turner syndrome contemplating pregnancy can be found in the International Turner Syndrome Consensus Group guidelines.
Many women with Turner syndrome are infertile, but with assisted reproduction they can achieve pregnancy at a rate similar to that of women infertile for other reasons.

Pregnancies in women with Turner syndrome have a higher risk of obstetric and non-obstetric complications, and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology recommends specialist management to include a cardiologist.
For women who have mosaic Turner syndrome and persistent ovarian function, oocyte cryopreservation after controlled ovarian hyperstimulation can be considered as a fertility preservation option.
Early diagnosis is optimal; hGH can be started as early as 6 months of age.

In one RCT of 123 girls with Turner syndrome who had reached puberty, girls who received low-dose ethinyl estradiol from age 5 years to 12 years vs. placebo had significantly earlier thelarche (median, 11.6 vs 12.6 years) and a slower tempo of puberty (median, 3.3 vs 2.2 years); both groups had delayed menarche (median, 15.0 years).
